newsitem.title: USA: Gulfstream looking for revenues to soar.
newsitem.headline: Gulfstream looking for revenues to soar.

text.p: Gulfstream Aerospace Corp., maker of the world's most popular corporate jet, expects revenues to soar over the next 12 months as its newest jet enters the skies.

"By late '97, early '98 we'll effectively double revenues," Gulfstream Vice Chairman Bryan Moss said in an interview before the inaguaral world tour of the company's new flagship the Gulfstream V (G-V).

"We're extremely comfortable with doubling of revenues from $1 billion to $2 billion ... what could drive any revenues beyond that would be what we do with production and that's pretty much set between now and 1999," he said.

Moss said the driving force behind the revenue growth is strong demand for the G-V, a luxury jet with a non-stop range of 6,500 nautical miles which makes non-stop flights from New York to Tokyo or London to Hong Kong a reality.

With over 70 G-V's sold to users and a backlog that runs to the start of the year 2000, Gulfstream expects to double production from 1996 levels to 60 aircraft a year by 1999. Moss feels even that projection could be conservative.
"I would say that in the next nine to 12 months we will take another look at whether 60 is the right number," he said. "I believe the number could be higher."

A continuing worldwide business expansion where highly paid executives are striving for shareholder value, diminished service from airlines for business travelers and, most importantly, fractional ownership of jets, are boosting demand for business jets, Moss said.

"Those three elements cause me to be more optimistic about the outlook for the industry, and therefore production, than I have ever been," Moss said. "The perception of the business aircraft has been more as a perk than as a business tool but I'm seeing a very big shift in that set of perceptions."

The G-V, which seats up to 19 in the sort of luxury that makes standard coach class seem inhuman, is in the process of receiving final approvals from the Federal Aviation Authority and will start service around the world this summer.
With a price between $35 million and $37 million, compared with about $28 million for a Gulfstream IV, the G-V is alone in that price range, bringing new meaning to the tag luxury jet.

"There is as lot of sticker-shock when people ask what is the price of an airplane like this," Moss said, but being a consumate salesman he quickly added even after using the plane for 15 years an owner could sell it for up to 90 percent of the original price.

Gulfstream won't be alone in the category for long. Within about one year Bombardier Inc. will launch its Global Express which bears a striking resemblance to the G-V in all categories including perfomance and price.
Moss, who was president of Bombardier's business jet division until 1995, feels the race for market leadership has already been won.
"We have at least a one year advantage on (Bombardier) and that's if they are able to meet the schedule that they are projecting," Moss said.
"Being first to the market with the G-V is a huge advantage," he said adding that while Bombardier has been using price as a selling point it has not been a concern for Gulfstream.

One concern for Gulfstream is new competition from Boeing Business Jets, the Boeing Co. and General Electric Co. luxury corporate jet joint venture launched last summer. Boeing Business is marketing a luxury derivative of the next generation 737-700 that will be able to fly over 6,000 nautical miles and has a bigger cabin.

"We have great respect for those two names so we are not being cavalier when we say we are not taking the 737 as a serious threat to any of the companies or prospects that we are currently working with," Moss said.

Moss said the fact that only a limited number of airports can accommodate the 737, which needs a longer runway than the G-V, makes the 737 less attractive, and besides, the Boeing/GE plane would cost between $2 milion and $4 million more than a G-V, Moss estimated, proving price can always be an issue if you're cheaper.
